Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Cerebellum controls timing of periaqueductal grey encoding of fear memory and expression of fear conditioned behaviour" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Roy V Sillitoe as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Senior Editor.

We are sorry to say that, after consultation with the reviewers, we have decided that your work, in its current form, will not be considered further for publication by eLife.

While all three Reviewers found the direction of the research and the results promising, there were a number of concerns raised. In a number of instances there is a requirement for better controls. In addition, clarification and deeper analyses were suggested for the electrophysiology and behavior experiments. The Reviewers felt that there was a dis-link between the reported histology data of where the accurately targeted electrodes/cannulas were placed and the robustness of the electrophysiology data. For the behavior, an increase in "n" is necessary in some cases, and a suggestion was made to verify that the aversive effect of the ataxia is not responsible of the changes in fear responses during extinction.

We would consider a revised manuscript as a new initial submission, provided you are able to well address all the comments and concerns raised by each reviewer.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, Lawrenson et al. have investigated the contribution of cerebellar projections to the ventral periaqueductal gray (vPAG) to fear-associated behaviors. The manuscript extends a prior, albeit incomplete, understanding of how the cerebellum mediates aversive conditioning via the PAG. In particular, the authors show that vPAG neurons respond both to conditioned stimulus onset and offset, but that there are likely 3 populations of neurons that participate in this response, Type 1, Type 1 onset, and Type 1 offset. They show that blocking cerebellar nuclear signaling with muscimol delivered to the medial cerebellar nucleus during consolidation preferentially effects the only vPAG signaling at offset. The correlate to this in terms of fear behavior was seen to be an increase in rearing during early extinction, with no changes seen in USV or freezing behaviors. The authors then extend their electrophysiology analysis by showing that at the population level, neurons in both the fastigial nucleus and the vPAG show alterations in firing amplitude at CS offset, but not onset, in late vs early extinction, further strengthening the case of involvement of the cerebellum in this process. Finally, the authors use inactivation of the fastigial to vPAG circuit during the acquisition phase using DREADD technology and show effects on freezing and USV behaviors. The manuscript does an elegant job of defining a key cerebellar pathway involved in fear and succeeds in broadening the role of the cerebellum beyond basic motor function. The main weaknesses of the results are related to the presentation of certain control data and in some cases a need for additional clarity in how the data were interpreted and presented.

(1) Experimental design and paradigm: Please include the timing of both DREADD injection and muscimol injection in the experimental design schematic in Figure 1a. Alongside this, there is some concern regarding the apparent break required in the timing of muscimol injection and washout in the experimental paradigm. This extends the paradigm from the 3 days described in methods (day 0, 1, 2) to 5 days (day 0, 1, (48 hour muscimol delay), day 2 (actually day 4)). Please clarify.

(2) There are some discrepancies in the figure legends and the methods regarding the number of controls. In the methods it is stated that there are 4 saline injected controls, while in the figure this number is stated as 8.

(3) As the pooled control electrophysiology data (as stated on page 4 lines 5-8) reflects both the 3 and 5 day paradigm, are similar changes seen in EE vs LE in all three groups (3 day control, 5 day saline control, 5 day muscimol experimental)? Adding PETH panels similar to Figures2/3 A & B to supplementary figure 2 would be helpful in this regard.

(4) vPAG offset responses during trace conditioning: While this is a well-designed control, these data appear too preliminary in their current form. Please increase the sample size.

(5) Muscimol effect on rearing behavior: Given the very low number of rearings observed in control animals, saline controls, DREADD, and vehicle animals I am left to wonder whether muscimol itself has an effect on rearing independent of the conditioning paradigm used. Is such data published and could that be cited? If not, what is the explanation for this? Clarification of this point would be useful especially as it is the only behavioral outcome associated with the muscimol paradigm.

(6) Please discuss and justify why only male animals were used.

(7) Please discuss why there is such a large amount of variability in the control condition as shown in Figure 5B for the inter-CS-US interval graph (bottom right).

(8) What is the level of inhibition achieved with the DREADD experiments? That is, after CNO, what does inhibition actually look like at the single cell level and/or at the local population level? What is the efficiency of inhibition after drug delivery?

(9) For the supplementary figures (and it would be helpful in all the other figures as well), for example supplementary figure 1, please show the actual histology and not just the schematized data. There seems to be some ambiguity in the locations and it is much more informative of the reader has the actual data to examine alongside the functional data.

Specific items:

1. Line 14: change "rat ventral (vPAG)" to "rat ventral PAG (vPAG)"

2. Please clarify whether the vPAG is a subsection of the longitudinal columns of the PAG – some readers may not have a detailed knowledge of this structure.

3. Figure 1C: Please make the red bar translucent, it is difficult to tell whether there is a peak being obscured or not.

4. Please refrain from using qualitative language where statistics are not done. Instead refer to the actual numbers (instead of "large majority (75%, n=24/32) use "75% (n=24/32)" or simply "majority"). Similarly regarding "small proportion (18.5%)…".

Reviewer #2:

This is an interesting study describing the interactions between the cerebellum and periaqueductal grey (PAG) in fear conditioning behavior in rats. To this end the authors first studied the PAG cellular responses during an auditory cued fear conditioning paradigm. Then, they performed global cerebellar inactivation with muscimol after fear conditioning, during consolidation period and they revealed ataxia in all animals and no difference during extinction training except for rearing behavior. They also performed chemogenetic experiments to inhibit cerebello-PAG pathway during acquisition and early consolidation and show effects on extinction rate of fear related freezing and ultrasonic vocalizations. The main findings are (1) a change in PAG response to the offset of the CS and an increase solely in rearing (but not freezing or vocalization) during the extinction phase following cerebellar inhibition immediately after the conditioning, (2) a reduction of vocalization and rate of extinction during the extinction phase following the selective inhibition of cerebellar terminals in the PAG. The introduction and discussion are clear and well written, the experiments seem carefully performed; yet the results seem a bit descriptive in the current state of the manuscript and the different elements that compose the manuscript are still a bit too loosely connected. There are notably several weaknesses which need to be addressed:

(1) In the experiments with muscimol in MCN (page 11), the infusion induced ataxia. This is a severe condition that likely induces intense stress and involves many structures. The interaction with the fear learning could thus result from an interference between the newly-formed memory and a muscimol-induced fear/stress. An effort to control for this effect would be needed to discard this alternate cause (e.g. could muscimol infusion in the interposed nucleus induce ataxia without affecting the cerebellum-PAG pathway? According to Teune et al. 2000 -cited in the manuscript- it does not seem to project heavily to the PAG).

(2) The results of figures 2 and 3 are presented in parallel, in a way that needlessly complicates the reading. The CS+ onset and CS+ offset neuronal responses are presented together with respectively the fear responses during and between the CS in separate figures but the link between the electrophysiological and behavioral responses is correlative (see point 4 below). A better presentation would be to provide separate figures for the electrophysiology and the behavior as in the text (or change the text).

(3) The behavioral analysis with n=4 rats (muscimol) does not have much sense given the variability of the behavior(s). More animals are needed for the behavior.

(4) The presence of a correspondence between the changes in electrophysiological and behavioral responses in each animal (explored by pairwise correlations) would reinforce the observations: are the animals with the weakest extinction showing weaker changes in the electrophysiological responses? (NB: page 7 line 2, the difference between the responses is not properly documented: a difference in significance in two conditions is not equivalent to a significant difference between the conditions).

(5) The physiological relevance of the neuronal discharge at the CS offset (where a cerebellar contribution is suspected) remains undefined. The experiments for vPAG offset responses during trace conditioning (page 11) is very interesting in light of the characterization of the offset response. Yet, this result is too anecdotal (only one animal) and not fully analyzed (no quantification for the EE and LE). The manuscript would benefit greatly from a proper demonstration of this response.

6) The ERP experiment is suffering from two limitations: (1) it is unclear how the LFP relates to the neuronal activity vs afferent activity; it would be much helpful to show using the available PAG recordings how the LFP relates to the multiunit activity. (2) the number of animals is too limited for the analysis (the lack of effect on MCN onset is only based on 4 pairs of measures in which 3 pairs show a clear decrement; btw: how is it possible to have 5 animals CS+ offset but only 4 in CS+ onset?); testing the covariance of MCN and PAG ERPs for each rat could help circumvent the limited number of animals (are the inter-trial fluctuations related in the two structures ?). More animals should be added otherwise.

7) It is difficult to judge from the specificity of the action of CNO; some cannulas (sup Figure 5, -7.5 AP) seem off-target (ventral PAG rather than vlPAG, while it contains very few cerebellar terminals according to sup Figure 4B): were these experiments included in the analysis? Terminal labeling has been found in the region bordering the vlPAG: how can the authors be sure that the behavioral effects are not due to an action on these terminals outside of the PAG? The diffusion of CNO needs to be documented to interpret these experiments.

8) If I understand correctly, the extended response to the CS-offset (Figure 3B) is interpreted as poor temporal patterning (discussion p22-23); the average trace indicates longer responses to CS+ offset after muscimol during consolidation; are these responses less precisely associated to the end of the CS ? Because the traces are only presented as a grand average, it is not possible to see whether some responses become poorly correlated to the end of the CS.

Reviewer #3:

The authors investigated the role of projections from the medial cerebellar nucleus (MCN) to the ventral periaqueductal gray (vPAG) in a conditioned fear learning task in rats, measuring vPAG neuronal activity and behavior before and after inhibiting MCN activity or the MCN-vPAG pathway. Inactivation of the MCN and the MCN – vPAG projections both affect fear learning related neuronal activity and behavior but in different ways. MCN inactivation results in a reduced neuronal response at the end of the conditioned tone stimulus, and also more frequent rearing and more frequent ultrasonic vocalizations during extinction. Neither manipulation changed the expression of fear as measured by freezing behavior, or the rate of fear extinction. Several statements in the manuscript are not supported by the results, such as the statement that the timing of neuronal activity signaling the end of the conditioned stimulus is altered by inhibition of the MCN or its projections.

The differences between the observed effects of the two manipulations (MCN or pathway inhibition) on fear learning may be due to the differences in the method and timing of inactivation. MCN is inactivated during consolidation. The MCN vPAC pathway is inhibited during fear acquisition, with inhibition possibly extending into early consolidation. MCN inhibition is through muscimol, pathway inhibition through use of and DREADDs. These differences introduce unknown variability into the results.

There is no description of measurements to determine how effective the inhibition of the MCN or the vPAC was, but interpretation of results is under the assumption that it was complete or near complete. While a systemic injection of CNO will deliver clozapine to all DREADD receptors (and, depending on does possibly also endogenous clozapine receptors), it does not inform about the percentage of projecting axons that express the designer receptor. It would have been reassuring to see some electrophysiological proof of the success and extent of the inhibition.

The authors don't seem to have performed necessary control experiments to exclude potential effects of CNO on endogenous clozapine binding sites in the brain when using systemic CNO injections.

The authors state that MCN inhibition alters the temporal precision of vPAG offset activity. Timing as a contribution of the cerebellum to fear learning is mentioned several times. However, there is no actual data supporting a change in timing or temporal precision. The authors don't analyze the temporal precision of the offset response, only the area under the curve and peak amplitude.

In the last paragraph of the introduction the authors claim that the rate of extinction is affected by MCN inhibition. There are no results to support this. In the same paragraph the authors state that ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) and rearing behavior during fear acquisition are influenced by MCN inputs to vPAC. However, all results for USV and rearing counts are shown for the extinction phase.

Experimental findings with an n = 1, as the author's experiment with one rat exposed to trace fear conditioning, are not acceptable.

Supplementary Figure 1 A is supposed to show electrode tracks for rats implanted with two drives for electrodes. The left cerebellar illustration shows what is declared as canular tracks in the other illustration. Was that by mistake or where cannulas inserted here?

The manuscript overstates several findings. For example, the presented findings do not imply that the cerebellum 'controls' any of these behaviors or activity patterns but rather that it is part of a larger circuit that does.

The claim that the cerebellum control aspects of timing in this task is not supported by results. The timing of the off response, which is specifically mentioned, needs to be analyzed to support or refute this claim.

The trace fear conditioning experiment should be repeated with at least two more animals (although a higher number would likely be needed).

Manipulations of MCN activity and of the MCN-vPAG pathway should occur during the same period in the fear conditioning protocol and preferentially by using the same method to ensure similar time courses.

Inhibition of the MCN and especially be confirmed electrophysiologically, at least for some examples.

Please show some example raw data of your electrophysiological recordings.

results.result: vlPAG neurons encode fear memory through temporally precise signaling of both CS+ onset and offset during retrieval. Type 1 units show phasic increases at both CS+ onset and offset, with 72.4% responding to both, 10.3% only to onset, and 17.3% only to offset. These responses are dependent on associative conditioning, as units showed little response during habituation.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C35-C40, C130, C132 provide converging evidence from electrophysiological recordings showing that vlPAG neurons encode both CS+ onset and offset with temporal precision. The data include specific percentages of unit types, statistical analyses, and comparison between habituation and conditioning phases. The sample sizes (29 type 1 units from 9 animals) and statistical significance (referenced in Figures 1D-E) support these findings.

results.result: CS+ onset and offset responses in vlPAG are mediated by independent mechanisms, as evidenced by differential extinction sensitivity and the existence of units responding exclusively to onset or offset.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C41, C45-C49, C131 demonstrate independence through multiple lines of evidence: (1) some units respond only to onset or offset, (2) extinction patterns differ between onset and offset responses (offset shows 67% decrease in peak z-score vs. 13.8% for onset), and (3) statistical analyses confirm these differences (p<0.05). The convergence of anatomical (separate unit populations) and functional (differential extinction) evidence strongly supports independence.

results.result: MCN inactivation during consolidation disrupts the temporal precision of vlPAG offset responses but not onset responses during subsequent retrieval. Muscimol infusion increased the number and altered latency of peaks at CS+ offset (82% of control peaks in 200ms vs. 20% in muscimol), while onset responses remained unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C78-C81, C84-C89, C134, C187, C189 provide strong evidence from muscimol inactivation experiments. The data show selective disruption of offset temporal precision (increased peak number: t(31)=7.184, p<0.0001; altered latency: χ²(4)=13.31, p<0.01) while onset responses were unchanged (Figure 4A-B). The specificity of the effect (offset but not onset) and statistical significance support the conclusion about MCN's role in timing offset responses.

results.result: MCN inactivation during consolidation increases the duration of individual freezing and movement bouts during retrieval without affecting overall freezing percentage. Freezing epochs were significantly longer in muscimol animals (EE: 26.45s vs. 9.2s control, p=0.014; LE: 9.1s vs. 3.4s control, p=0.026).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C97-C102, C142-C143 demonstrate that MCN inactivation affects temporal structure but not overall fear expression. Statistical analyses show significant increases in bout duration (Mann-Whitney tests, p<0.05) while percentage freezing remains unchanged (C91-C92). The dissociation between bout duration and overall freezing percentage is well-documented with appropriate statistics, supporting the conclusion about MCN's role in temporal patterning of behavior.

results.result: Chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG pathway during acquisition reduces fear-related ultrasonic vocalizations by 36% during the inter-trial interval (ITI) but not during CS-US presentations.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C115-C116, C144, C204 show a specific effect on USVs during ITI (36% reduction, U=23, p=0.032, one-tailed Mann-Whitney test) but not during CS-US presentations (U=39, p=0.310). The statistical significance, specificity of the effect (ITI but not CS-US), and appropriate sample sizes (n=9-10 per group) support this finding. However, the high variability in USV expression noted in the manuscript (C125) should be considered.

results.result: Chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG pathway during acquisition slows the extinction rate of fear-related freezing during CS+ presentation (t(17)=2.01, p=0.042) but not during ITI, suggesting a specific effect on cue-related extinction rather than general freezing behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C121-C123, C140, C208 demonstrate a selective effect on extinction rate during CS+ (p=0.042) but not ITI (p=0.229). The specificity argues against a general motor or anxiety effect. The finding is consistent with previous mouse studies (C139, Frontera et al., 2020), providing cross-species validation. Statistical significance and appropriate controls support this conclusion.

results.result: In trace conditioning experiments, vlPAG offset responses follow CS+ offset timing rather than US timing, with no statistical difference in time to peak between delay and trace conditioning (t(25)=1.76, p=0.091).
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C168, C184 provide evidence from trace conditioning experiments (n=6 type 1 offset units, n=6 type 4 offset units) showing that offset responses track CS+ offset (~30ms after tone end) rather than expected US timing. The lack of statistical difference between delay and trace conditions (p=0.091) supports this interpretation. However, the authors acknowledge the 1s trace interval may have been too short for discrimination (C185), which is a reasonable caveat.

results.result: Population activity in MCN and vlPAG, measured by ERPs, shows differential patterns at CS+ onset versus offset. Onset ERPs show no extinction-related changes, while offset ERPs in vlPAG show 65% amplitude reduction (p=0.007). ERP amplitudes correlate between MCN and vlPAG (onset: rrm=0.64, p<0.0001; offset: rrm=0.44, p=0.033).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C70 provide comprehensive ERP data from 6 animals showing: (1) differential latencies suggesting separate pathways for onset vs. offset, (2) selective extinction effects on offset but not onset ERPs, and (3) significant correlations between MCN and vlPAG. The statistical analyses are appropriate (paired t-tests, repeated-measures correlation), and the convergence with single-unit data (C70) strengthens the findings. Sample size (n=6) is modest but adequate for within-subject comparisons.

results.result: vlPAG unit responses at CS+ onset and offset correlate with freezing behavior within individual animals (onset: rrm=0.38-0.58, p<0.05; offset: rrm=0.55-0.69, p<0.01) but do not predict individual differences in overall freezing magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 show significant within-animal correlations using repeated-measures correlation, consistent with previous literature (Ozawa et al., 2016; Wright and McDannald, 2019). However, the lack of correlation between absolute changes in unit response and freezing (C105) indicates these signals reflect state rather than trait differences. The statistical approach (repeated-measures correlation) is appropriate for within-subject relationships, and the interpretation is appropriately nuanced.

results.result: Anatomical tracing demonstrates direct MCN-to-vlPAG projections, with terminal labeling primarily in contralateral vlPAG. Double-labeling shows 70±10.2% of PAG-projecting MCN neurons were DREADD-transfected.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 provide anatomical validation for the pathway manipulation experiments. The anterograde tracing (n=7 rats) consistently shows contralateral vlPAG targeting, and double-labeling (n=4 rats) confirms substantial DREADD transfection of the relevant projection neurons (70% of PAG-projecting population). These data validate the specificity of the DREADD manipulation, though the 28% transfection rate relative to total DREADD population suggests some off-target effects are possible.

results.result: During acquisition and extinction, DREADD and control animals show similar levels of freezing behavior during CS-US presentations and ITI, with both groups demonstrating comparable extinction learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114, C117-C120 show no differences in freezing percentages between groups using appropriate statistical tests (two-way repeated-measures ANOVA for acquisition, unpaired t-tests for extinction). The lack of difference in overall freezing levels, combined with the specific effect on extinction rate (C121), suggests the manipulation affects learning dynamics rather than fear expression per se. Sample sizes (n=9-10 per group) and statistical approaches are appropriate.

results.result: Muscimol infusion into MCN induced transient ataxia (resolving within 24hr) but did not affect overall vlPAG firing rates during extinction (control vs. muscimol: t(78)=0.407, p=0.685) or CS+ onset responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C76-C77 provide important controls showing that muscimol effects were specific rather than due to general neural suppression. The ataxia confirms drug efficacy, while the lack of effect on firing rates and onset responses demonstrates specificity. Statistical comparisons are appropriate, though the authors acknowledge that stress from ataxia could potentially confound results (discussed in Methods). The 48hr delay before testing helps mitigate this concern.

results.result: MCN inactivation during consolidation does not affect the overall percentage of time spent freezing or the rate of extinction during CS+ presentation or ITI in subsequent retrieval sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95, C141 show consistent lack of effects on freezing percentage and extinction rate using appropriate statistical tests (paired and unpaired t-tests, all p>0.05). This dissociation between temporal structure (bout duration, C97-C101) and overall freezing amount is well-documented and strengthens the interpretation that MCN affects timing rather than fear intensity. Sample sizes (n=8-10 per group) are adequate.

results.result: MCN manipulations (muscimol during consolidation or DREADD during acquisition) did not affect rearing behavior or USVs during extinction training.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108, C124-C125 report null findings for rearing and USVs during extinction using appropriate non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney). While null results require cautious interpretation, the consistency across both manipulation types and the specificity of effects on other measures (freezing bout duration, extinction rate) suggest these are genuine null findings rather than lack of power. However, the high variability in USVs noted by authors is a limitation.

results.result: Control behavioral tests (elevated plus maze, open field, beam walking) showed no differences between DREADD and control animals following CNO infusion into vlPAG, but intraperitoneal CNO produced ataxia and impaired beam walking in DREADD animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C129 provide important controls demonstrating that targeted MCN-PAG pathway modulation does not cause general motor or anxiety deficits (all p>0.05), while systemic CNO confirms DREADD efficacy through cerebellar effects (beam walking: t(16)=3.192, p=0.006). This dissociation validates the specificity of the intracranial CNO manipulation. However, the authors appropriately note that insufficient DREADD effect cannot be ruled out (C127).

results.result: Characterization of vlPAG unit responses across fear conditioning phases: During habituation (32 units, 8 animals), 75% were unresponsive to tone. During acquisition (50 units, 10 animals), 18.5% responded to CS onset and 20% to US. During retrieval/extinction (55 units, 10 animals), 52.7% showed type 1 responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C34 provide systematic characterization of unit responses across conditioning phases with clear sample sizes and percentages. The progression from minimal habituation responses to robust conditioned responses supports the associative nature of the learning. Statistical analyses are appropriate (z-score normalization, significance threshold of ±2 SD). This descriptive characterization is essential for interpreting the main findings.

results.result: Classification of vlPAG unit types during extinction: 40% type 2 (no response), 7% type 4 (decreased firing), no type 3 (biphasic). In muscimol experiments, 71% of type 1 onset units showed extinction-related reduction in integrated response area.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C74-C75 provide systematic classification using established criteria (Watson et al., 2016). The percentages and statistical analyses (paired t-tests) are clearly reported. The consistency of extinction patterns between control and muscimol animals for onset responses (C74-C75) strengthens the specificity of the offset effects. Classification criteria are well-defined in methods.

results.result: After CS+ onset, there were no significant differences between muscimol and control animals in the number of peaks (EE: t(36)=1.570, p=0.125; LE: t(37)=0.651, p=0.519) or latency to peak (χ²(4)=2.50, p=0.645), with ~85% of peaks occurring within 200ms of CS+ onset in both groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 provide detailed temporal analysis showing preserved onset response characteristics despite MCN inactivation. The use of both parametric (t-test) and non-parametric (chi-square) statistics is appropriate for the different measures. The high proportion of early peaks (85%) in both groups demonstrates temporal precision is maintained for onset responses, contrasting with the disruption seen for offset responses (C84-C87).

results.result: At baseline (before extinction training), there were no differences in freezing or movement epoch duration between control and muscimol animals (freezing: U=19, p=0.195; movement: U=38, p=0.877).
results.evaluation: Claim C96 provides an essential baseline control showing that groups were equivalent before CS+ presentation. The use of non-parametric statistics (Mann-Whitney) is appropriate for the likely non-normal distribution of bout durations. This baseline equivalence strengthens the interpretation that subsequent differences (C97-C99) are due to MCN manipulation effects on fear memory consolidation rather than pre-existing differences.

results.result: The cerebellum, through MCN, regulates fear memory processes at multiple timescales: millisecond-level control of CS+ offset encoding in vlPAG, and longer timescales (seconds to days) affecting freezing bout duration, extinction rate, and timing of fear-related behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C145, C199-C202, C211-C212 synthesize findings across multiple experiments showing multi-timescale regulation. The millisecond-level effects are demonstrated by altered peak timing (C84-C87), while longer-timescale effects include bout duration (C97-C101) and extinction rate (C121). The convergence of evidence from different experimental approaches (muscimol, DREADD) and measures (neural, behavioral) strongly supports this integrative conclusion, which represents a major conceptual advance.

results.result: Dysfunctional interactions in the cerebellar-survival network may underlie fear-related disorders such as PTSD, with potential implications for understanding anxiety-like behavioral phenotypes and extinction deficits.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C210 are explicitly speculative ("raising the possibility," "may contribute") and extend beyond the experimental data. While the findings on extinction rate and temporal patterning are relevant to PTSD (which involves extinction deficits, C23), the experiments were conducted in healthy male rats with acute manipulations. Establishing clinical relevance would require additional studies examining chronic dysfunction, female subjects, and validation in clinical populations. The speculation is reasonable but unsupported by the current data.

results.result: Background claims about PAG and cerebellar roles in fear behavior, based on previous literature: vlPAG mediates freezing, USVs, and rearing; cerebellar vermis/MCN contribute to fear-related behaviors; cerebellum is connected to survival networks including vlPAG across species; extinction deficits relate to PTSD and chronic pain.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C24 are well-supported by extensive citations to previous literature. These provide essential context for the current study and are appropriately referenced. The authors correctly cite established findings about PAG function (C11-C14), cerebellar contributions to fear (C15-C19), anatomical connectivity (C20-C21), and clinical relevance (C23-C24). These knowledge claims are not novel findings but necessary background.

results.result: Comparison to previous literature: Prior studies showed cerebellar involvement in fear memory consolidation (Sacchetti et al., 2002, 2007) and MCN-PAG pathway effects on extinction (Frontera et al., 2020). CS+ onset responses were previously reported, but temporally precise offset responses are novel. Methodological differences (bin width, tone characteristics) may explain why offset responses were not detected previously.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C151 provide appropriate contextualization of findings relative to prior work. The authors correctly identify the novelty of the offset responses (C147) and provide plausible methodological explanations for why they weren't detected previously (C148-C151). The comparison to Frontera et al., 2020 (C139) shows cross-species consistency. The discussion of bin width (40ms vs. 1s, C150-C151) is a valid methodological point supported by the data.

results.result: Discussion of CS+ onset response mechanisms and comparison to ramping units: Onset responses may be generated by amygdala input and encode multiple aspects of fear processing. The current findings are consistent with Watson et al., 2016. Ramping units (Wright & McDannald, 2019) differ from the phasic offset responses observed here, likely due to paradigm differences (trace conditioning with variable US probability).
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C166 provide thorough comparison to previous electrophysiological studies with appropriate citations. The distinction between phasic offset responses and ramping units (C160-C163) is clearly articulated and supported by methodological differences (C165-C166). The acknowledgment that current onset findings are consistent with prior work (C159) is appropriate. This scholarly discussion properly situates the findings within existing literature.

results.result: Discussion of potential neural pathways generating CS+ offset responses: Offset responses occur ~30ms after CS+ end, allowing multiple possible pathways. Auditory cortex shows onset/offset responses but projects to dorsolateral PAG (flight-related). Medial prefrontal cortex and bed nucleus of stria terminalis are alternative candidates with appropriate projections and sustained CS+ activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C176 present reasonable speculation about neural pathways but lack direct experimental evidence. The timing estimate (C168) is data-based, but pathway identification requires additional experiments (tracing, inactivation, or optogenetics). The authors appropriately acknowledge this is "an unanswered question" (C167) and present multiple possibilities with supporting citations. The speculation is well-reasoned but the pathways remain unidentified, making this uncertain rather than supported or unsupported.

results.result: Discussion of whether offset responses encode prediction error: Learning theory predicts extinction-related reduction in prediction error signals. The gradual reduction in offset responses during extinction is consistent with prediction error encoding. However, trace conditioning results (responses follow CS+ offset, not US timing) argue against this interpretation, though the 1s interval may have been too short for discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C186 present conflicting evidence about prediction error encoding. The extinction pattern (C183) supports the hypothesis, but trace conditioning results (C184) argue against it. The authors appropriately acknowledge both interpretations and note methodological limitations (C185). Alternative interpretations (saliency signaling, C186) are mentioned. Without additional experiments (e.g., longer trace intervals, explicit prediction error manipulations), the functional significance remains uncertain despite the clear phenomenology.

results.result: Discussion of MCN-vlPAG interactions and timing hypothesis: MCN inactivation disrupts but doesn't abolish offset responses, consistent with MCN modulating vlPAG activity. The apparent contradiction from ERP latencies (PAG earlier than MCN) is explained by manipulation during consolidation affecting subsequent retrieval. Temporal pattern of activation matters (phasic vs. tonic). Findings extend cerebellar timing hypothesis to fear memory encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C198 provide thoughtful integration of findings with cerebellar timing theory. The explanation for ERP latency paradox (C190-C191) is reasonable given the consolidation manipulation. The connection to timing hypothesis (C195-C198) is well-supported by citations and consistent with the multi-timescale effects observed. The discussion of temporal patterns (C192-C194) is supported by Frontera et al., 2020. This represents appropriate theoretical integration of the findings.

results.result: Discussion of MCN effects on different fear behaviors: MCN indirectly influences freezing during extinction but more directly affects USVs during acquisition. The MCN-PAG pathway may regulate USVs when danger is greatest. Activity during acquisition affects subsequent extinction rate, with potential implications for individual differences in extinction phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C209 synthesize behavioral findings with appropriate citations. The distinction between indirect (freezing) and direct (USV) effects is supported by the data patterns. The connection to individual differences (C209, citing Ji et al., 2018) is reasonable speculation based on the extinction rate findings. The USV interpretation (C207) is speculative but grounded in the data and previous literature (C206). The integration is appropriate though some elements remain speculative.

results.result: Overarching conclusion: The cerebellum, through interactions with the survival network, coordinates the most appropriate behavioral response at the most appropriate time.
results.evaluation: Claim C213 represents a high-level synthesis of the findings. While speculative in tone ("might therefore be"), it is well-supported by the convergent evidence of multi-timescale regulation (C199-C202), phase-specific effects (C145, C212), and temporal precision effects (C5, C134). The conclusion appropriately captures the main conceptual advance of the work: demonstrating cerebellar involvement in temporal coordination of fear responses across multiple timescales.

results.result: Methodological details: All procedures were approved by University of Bristol ethics committee (PPL: PA26B438F) and complied with UK Animals Act 1986. A total of 47 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (280-400g) were used.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C215 provide essential methodological information about ethical approval and subjects. These are straightforward factual statements that are appropriately documented. The limitation to male subjects is noted, with the authors acknowledging this as a limitation in the discussion. The sample size across all experiments is adequate for the statistical analyses performed.
